analogs.covers: The main animal and the whole day: the big gull of the Baltic beach that sits for hours on sand, groynes and rocks, walks the tideline, follows every boat and walker, snatches food from other animals, chases crows and rivals off its find and drops mussels onto stone to crack them

The water half: a diving fisher of shallow coasts, lagoons and estuaries that swims after its fish, sits on posts and rocks with its wings spread to dry and roosts and nests in colonies with water all around

headline: A Baltic beach gull with a cormorant's dive: sits on sand and rocks, raids every kill on the shore, cracks mussels on stone and turns into a pack hunter at night.

setting.label: Beaches, mudflats, swamps, islands and the coast inland to the bogs
setting.note: Beaches and brushy coast (Tallbrush Coasts), the islands (Palm Islands, Volcano Islands), the mudflats, the Coastland Swamp and the East Passage, plus the wet woods and bogs it follows land animals into (Twisted Forest, Stillwater Bog, Big Tree Overlook). Shares the sea cliffs of the Coastal Bluffs with the ocean variant. Rests on sandbanks, rocks and islets in the shallows.

playsLike: You are the gull of Gondwa's beaches. Your day happens on the ground and just above it: you sit with your cluster on a sandbank, a rock or an islet in the shallows, walk the tideline for shells and scraps, and hop up only to move a few metres, harass a herbivore or dive-bomb a kill. Every predator on the beach is your provider: you follow it, wait at a distance and swoop on the claimed carcass the moment you dare, at your own risk. You drop mussels onto rocks, chase other scavengers off your food and dive into the shallows for fish like a cormorant, then dry your spread wings on a rock. At night the cheeky gull becomes a hunter: with up to four of you, you circle sleeping prey up to Medium, clack your beaks and peck in turns.

why.text: Tropeognathus are "highly opportunistic, opting to divebomb a claimed corpse when they spot one, regardless of whatever predator has it." That is the gull that steals a fish sandwich out of your hand on the promenade (official inspiration: seagulls).

They "comb the beaches and oceans for both potential prey and opportunities to scavenge" and eat "bones, fruit and insects when fish or meat is not available": the herring gull's tideline walk, on which almost anything edible counts.

"They take these objects high into the sky before dropping them, letting them smash on the ground below to crack them open for a tasty meal." Herring gulls do exactly this with mussels on rocks, piers and car parks.

"Herbivorous species are pursued and harassed - with air snaps common as they fly around them, hoping to provoke a chase for their own amusement." Carnivores they follow more warily, as gulls trail walkers and fishing boats.
"Tropeognathus do not tolerate scavengers, and will readily swoop and peck to chase them away." Gulls drive crows and rival gulls off their find; Rhamphorhynchus plays the crow.
They dive for fish and "bask for short periods of time, extending their wings to dry them out in the sun", like a cormorant on a post (official inspiration).
"They prefer to sleep somewhere surrounded by water - ideally a rock, small island, or coastal cliffside", as gulls and cormorants roost on sandbanks and rocks in the shallows.

notLike: Gulls don't hunt big animals at night; you become a coordinated pack hunter after dark.

A gull will stand on one beach for half a day. The profile says you get "restless if grounded for too long": you rest a lot on the ground, but you keep hopping from rock to sandbank to the next carcass.
twist: The beach version of the profile: more gull on the ground, less ocean wanderer in the sky. Your ocean cousin, the Sturmsegler, is the same animal as an albatross.
